What Is a Typing Speed Test?

A typing speed test is a standardized evaluation that measures how quickly and accurately you can transcribe text using a keyboard. Unlike casual typing, a structured test isolates your raw throughput under controlled conditions, giving you a reproducible performance benchmark you can track over time.

Modern typing tests support multiple modes including random words, real-world paragraphs, famous quotes, programming snippets, scientific terminology, number sequences, and symbol patterns to simulate the diverse typing demands of professional work environments.

How WPM Is Calculated

The Standard Formula

The globally accepted standard defines one word as exactly five characters, regardless of actual word length. This normalization ensures consistent comparison across languages, keyboard layouts, and content types.

Gross WPM = (Total Typed Characters divided by 5) divided by Time Elapsed in Minutes
Net WPM = (Correct Characters divided by 5) divided by Time Elapsed in Minutes
Accuracy = (Correct Characters divided by Total Typed Characters) multiplied by 100

Gross WPM vs. Net WPM

Gross WPM counts every character you type, including errors. Net WPM counts only correctly typed characters, providing a truer reflection of your productive output. This test calculates and displays Net WPM so your score is never artificially inflated by uncorrected mistakes.

Average Typing Speed Benchmarks

Understanding where your speed sits relative to global benchmarks helps you set realistic improvement goals:

  • 1 to 39 WPM — Beginner: Typical of those learning to type or who type with fewer than four fingers.
  • 40 to 59 WPM — Average: The global average for casual typists who have developed basic keyboard habits.
  • 60 to 79 WPM — Proficient: Comfortable for most professional roles. Emails, reports, and documents feel effortless.
  • 80 to 119 WPM — Speed Typist: Well above average. Developers, writers, and power users typically fall in this range.
  • 120+ WPM — Blazing Fast: Elite territory. Professional court reporters and competitive typists regularly exceed 120 WPM.

Tips to Improve Your Typing Speed

1. Accuracy Before Speed

Chasing speed while making frequent errors trains bad habits. Every mistake you make at high speed must later be unlearned. Start deliberately slow, aiming for 98 percent accuracy, then allow speed to develop naturally through repetition.

2. Use All Ten Fingers

Many self-taught typists rely on six or fewer fingers, creating cognitive bottlenecks. Training all ten fingers to handle their assigned keyboard zones distributes the load evenly, unlocking dramatic speed improvements over time.

3. Practice with Varied Content

Exclusive practice on common short words builds a limited skill set. Use this test multiple modes including quotes, technology, programming, science, numbers, and symbols to develop fluency across the full character range your work demands.

4. Consistent Short Sessions Beat Marathon Practice

Research on skill acquisition consistently shows that fifteen to thirty minutes of focused daily practice produces more durable improvements than occasional two-hour sessions. The brain consolidates muscle memory during rest periods between practice sessions.

Touch Typing Guide: The Foundation of Fast Typing

Touch typing is the technique of typing using all ten fingers without looking at the keyboard, relying entirely on muscle memory . It is the single most impactful skill you can develop to break through speed plateaus.

  • Master the Home Row: Rest your left fingers on A S D F and your right fingers on J K L semicolon. The raised bumps on F and J are your tactile anchors. Always return to this position after every keystroke sequence.
  • Assign Keys to Fingers: Each finger is responsible for a specific column of keys. Never reach across with the wrong finger. This discipline is what makes touch typing faster than hunt-and-peck at scale.
  • Keep Your Eyes on the Screen: Resist glancing at the keyboard. Cover your hands with a cloth if needed during early training. Visual dependency on keys is a hard habit to break the longer it persists.
  • Maintain Neutral Posture: Sit with your back straight, elbows at approximately ninety degrees, and wrists hovering slightly above the keyboard. Poor ergonomics causes fatigue that caps your speed and can damage joints over time.

Difficulty Levels and Typing Modes Explained

This test offers six difficulty levels for word mode, each calibrated to build progressively more demanding muscle memory patterns:

  • Easy: High-frequency two-to-four-letter words. Ideal for beginners building foundational habits.
  • Medium: Common five-to-eight-letter words appearing in everyday professional writing.
  • Hard: Multi-syllable vocabulary encountered in formal documents and academic writing.
  • Expert: Uncommon, sophisticated vocabulary drawn from literature and advanced discourse.
  • Impossible: Technical and scientific terminology including long compound words that challenge even elite typists.
  • Random: A chaotic blend of all difficulty levels, simulating the unpredictable vocabulary range of real-world typing tasks.

Beyond words, you can test yourself on real paragraph content from technology, programming, science, and fiction; on number sequences that simulate data-entry scenarios; and on symbol patterns that mirror code punctuation and special character requirements.

Useful Typing Resources

Looking to practice more or learn touch typing from scratch? Check out these excellent free resources:

  • TypingClub — Comprehensive touch typing courses for all skill levels.
  • Monkeytype — Highly customizable minimalistic typing test.
  • Keybr — Algorithm-based typing practice focusing on weak keys.
  • 10FastFingers — Competitive typing tests and multiplayer typing races.
  • TypeRacer — A gamified typing competition where you race cars by typing.
